images.description: The Pung cholom is a Manipuri dance. It is the soul of Manipuri Sankirtana music and Classical Manipuri dance. The Pung Cholom is a unique classical dance of Manipur. This dance may be performed by men or women and is usually a prelude to the Ras Lila. In this style, the dancers play the pung (a form of hand beaten drum) while they dance at the same time. Dancers need to be graceful and acrobatic

images.description: Lai Haraoba is a public festival in Manipur, India celebrated to please traditional deities. The festival is in part a recollection of the creation stories played the deities with the first origin of this universe and evolution of the plants and animals through the will of Atiya Shidaba.[1] Translated, Lai Haraoba means "merry making of the Gods."[

profile.name: Thougal Jagoi
profile.tagline: A dedication dance of the Meitei people performed for the deities of the Lai Haraoba.
profile.insight: Dancers are strictly forbidden from making eye contact with the audience; failing to maintain this boundary is considered a sacrilege against the deities being invoked.
profile.profile: Thougal Jagoi, also known as Jagoi Ashangbi, is a traditional Meitei dance of dedication performed during the Lai Haraoba religious festival in Manipur. It is a communal invocation involving men, women, and maibis (priestesses) who dance to please the deities. The performance typically lasts thirty minutes and serves as a prelude to the Hoi Lauba ceremony.
profile.profile_long:
Thougal Jagoi, which translates literally to the 'Dance of Dedication,' is a fundamental component of the Lai Haraoba, the ritual festival of the Meitei people of Manipur. Known alternatively as Jagoi Ashangbi, it functions as a collective offering to the deities. Unlike some ritual dances reserved solely for the maibis (priestesses), Thougal Jagoi is performed by a combined group of men and women alongside the priestesses, emphasizing the communal nature of the invocation. 

The performance is governed by strict ritual protocols. Dancers must adhere to a code of conduct where eye contact with the spectators is forbidden, as the dance is directed toward the divine rather than for human entertainment. Breaking this gaze is viewed as a sacrilege. The dance typically occupies a thirty-minute window within the festival's complex sequence of rituals. Following the conclusion of the Thougal Jagoi, the participants transition into the Hoi Lauba ceremony, a specific ritualistic enactment that continues the festival's progression. As part of the broader Jagoi tradition, it shares the refined, fluid aesthetic characteristic of Meitei culture, contributing to the foundational movements that eventually informed the classical Manipuri dance forms.

sections.origins_and_history: Thougal Jagoi is rooted in the ancient Sanamahist traditions of the Meitei people. It is a primary element of the Lai Haraoba festival, which celebrates the creation of the universe and the ancestors. The dance is categorized as an early form of Meitei dance that has contributed to the classical wealth of Manipur's culture.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed by men, women, and maibis. Dancers must strictly avoid eye contact with the audience. The movements are part of an invocatory sequence to please the lords. Technique details such as specific footwork are not described in the provided sources, but it is performed as a group for approximately thirty minutes.
sections.music_and_instruments: While the specific instrumentation for Thougal Jagoi is not detailed in the source, the broader Lai Haraoba festival context utilizes the pena (a traditional stringed instrument) and tunes that accompany the maibis' movements.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dance is performed in the context of the Lai Haraoba festival, typically in front of the shrine of the deities or in the open ritual space designated for the festival.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The name means 'Dance of dedication.' It is performed to invoke and please the deities during the Lai Haraoba. It serves as a spiritual preparation for the Hoi Lauba ceremony that follows.
sections.notable_figures: The maibis (priestesses) are the central ritual figures who lead the dance alongside the lay men and women of the community.
sections.regional_variants: The source mentions it as a Meitei traditional dance form within the context of the Lai Haraoba, which is celebrated across Meitei settlements.
sections.lineage: Thougal Jagoi belongs to the Jagoi tradition of Manipur, which includes other ritual forms like Leisem Jagoi and Laiching Jagoi.

profile.sacred_note: Dancers are strictly forbidden from making eye contact with the audience; doing so is considered a sacrilege.

Maintain a downward or internal gaze to avoid eye contact with spectators
Perform invocatory movements alongside maibis for thirty minutes
Conclude the dance to begin the Hoi Lauba ceremony
